# Necessity as attainability of an outcome target {#necessity}

A necessity claim asserts that an outcome target is unattainable below some level of a condition. A condition `X` is necessary for an outcome target `y` when no case reaches `Y >= y` below a required level of `X` [@Dul2016; @Dul2020]. The claim is asymmetric, because a case may hold the required level of the condition and still miss the target when other constraints hold the outcome down [@BraumoellerGoertz2000; @GoertzStarr2003].

The asymmetry gives a necessity claim a distinct signature in a scatter plot of the condition against the outcome. Cases with a low condition and a high outcome contradict the claim, and the upper-left corner of the scatter is therefore empty [@Dul2016]. Cases with a high condition and a low outcome agree with the claim, because a necessary condition permits failure above the requirement. Accounts of necessary conditions in set-theoretic methods describe the same asymmetry as a subset relation of the outcome to the condition [@Ragin2008; @SchneiderWagemann2012].

The guide uses the synthetic dataset of 200 cases of the `qnca` repository, whose condition and outcome lie on a scale from 0 to 100.

```{r necessity-data}
library(qnca)
d <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MarekDejaUJ/qnca/main/data/qnca_dataset_n200.csv")
summary(d)
```

The scatter of the 200 cases shows the reverse-L pattern of a necessary condition: the cases fill the lower-right triangle, and the upper-left corner holds no case.

```{r necessity-scatter, fig.cap = "The 200 cases of the synthetic dataset. The upper-left corner, with a low condition and a high outcome, holds no case."}
ggplot(d, aes(X, Y)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.2, colour = "grey25") +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 100), ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(x = "Condition X", y = "Outcome Y")
```

## The strict requirement of a target

For a target `y`, the strict requirement is the lowest condition value among the cases that reach the target. The requirement for the target 50 follows from the cases with `Y >= 50`.

```{r necessity-strict}
min(d$X[d$Y >= 50])
qnca_frontier(d$X, d$Y, pi = 1, y_grid = 50)
```

Both lines give the same value, because the QNCA frontier at the tolerance `pi = 1` is the lowest condition value among the successful cases. The value is the CE-FDH ceiling of NCA at the target 50 [@Dul2016]. Every case with `Y >= 50` holds at least the required level of `X`, and the strict requirement rests on the single case with the lowest condition value among the successful cases.

## A requirement with a stated tolerance

Quantile Necessary Condition Analysis (QNCA) reports a low quantile of the condition among the successful cases [@Deja2026QNCA]. The tolerance `pi` fixes the share `1 - pi` of the successful cases that may sit below the reported requirement. The requirement for the target 50 at `pi = 0.95` admits five percent of the successful cases below the reported level.

```{r necessity-tolerant}
req <- qnca_frontier(d$X, d$Y, pi = 0.95, y_grid = 50)
req
attain <- d$Y >= 50
c(successful = sum(attain), below = sum(d$X[attain] < req))
```

The tolerant requirement lies above the strict requirement, and the cases below the tolerant requirement form a small share of the successful cases. At the target 50, the share of successful cases below the requirement stays within the tolerance `1 - pi`. The reading of the requirement changes with the tolerance: at `pi = 1` the requirement marks the lowest observed success, and at `pi = 0.95` the requirement marks a level that at least ninety-five percent of the successful cases reach.

## The same call in Python and Julia

The Python package `qnca` and the Julia package `QuantileNecessity` compute the same requirements on the same data.

```{python necessity-python}
from urllib.request import urlopen
import numpy as np
from qnca import qnca_frontier

url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MarekDejaUJ/qnca/main/data/qnca_dataset_n200.csv"
X, Y = np.loadtxt(urlopen(url), delimiter=",", skiprows=1, unpack=True)
print(qnca_frontier(X, Y, pi=1.0, y_grid=np.array([50.0])))
print(qnca_frontier(X, Y, pi=0.95, y_grid=np.array([50.0])))
```

```{julia necessity-julia}
using QuantileNecessity, Downloads, DelimitedFiles

url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MarekDejaUJ/qnca/main/data/qnca_dataset_n200.csv"
data = readdlm(Downloads.download(url), ',', Float64; skipstart = 1)
X, Y = data[:, 1], data[:, 2]
println(qnca_frontier(X, Y, 1.0, [50.0]))
println(qnca_frontier(X, Y, 0.95, [50.0]))
```

A necessity claim stays a claim about attainability. A requirement above the observed level of a case predicts failure of the case at the target, and a requirement below the observed level of a case leaves the outcome of the case to the other conditions of the outcome [@Dul2016].
